props.title: In Like Flint

sections.content: In Like Flint stands as a delightfully absurd spy parody that perfectly captures the excess of 1960s spy-mania. Following the success of Our Man Flint (1966), James Coburn returns as the impossibly talented Derek Flint, this time investigating a feminist conspiracy to take over the world. The film deliberately amplifies the macho swagger of James Bond films like Thunderball (1965) and You Only Live Twice (1967), turning Flint into an even more exaggerated super-agent who can do everything from speaking dolphin to performing ballet.

sections.content: The film's production design by Jack Martin Smith and Walter M. Scott perfectly embodies the ultra-mod aesthetic that defined 1960s spy films. Like Modesty Blaise (1966) and Danger: Diabolik (1968), In Like Flint embraces pop art sensibilities with elaborate sets, futuristic gadgets, and fashion that screams Space Age optimism. The women's spa that serves as the villains' headquarters particularly exemplifies this style, mixing luxury with retrofuturistic technology.

While the film's sexual politics feel dated today, its influence on the spy parody genre remains significant. Movies like Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery (1997) and OSS 117: Cairo, Nest of Spies (2006) clearly draw from the Flint films' template of exaggerating spy tropes to the point of absurdity while maintaining slick production values. sections.content: In Like Flint emerged during a distinctive period when Hollywood attempted to create American alternatives to James Bond. While Bond dominated with films like From Russia with Love (1963) and Goldfinger (1964), American studios responded with deliberately lighter takes on the genre. The Matt Helm series starring Dean Martin and the Flint films with James Coburn offered a specifically American swagger, mixing comedy with spy action in ways that influenced later films like True Lies (1994).
